summary.text: The biological pump is the ocean's biologically driven movement of carbon from the air and land runoff into the deep ocean and seafloor sediments.
Phytoplankton fix carbon in the sunlit surface, and when organisms die their particles sink, often clumping into aggregates that fall much faster.
It moves about 10.2 gigatonnes of carbon into the ocean interior each year, and without it atmospheric carbon dioxide would be about 400 ppm higher.

facts.label: Reaching the seabed
facts.value: About 1% of particles leaving the surface

facts.label: Time in sediment
facts.value: May be stored for millions of years

items.prompt: Imagine the ocean's living things stopped carrying carbon down into the deep. What would happen to carbon dioxide in the air?

options.label: It would fall sharply
It would stay about the same
It would be much higher
It would only change by season

items.explain: An ocean without a biological pump would leave atmospheric carbon dioxide about 400 ppm higher than today.

items.prompt: Dead plankton and droppings often stick together into clumps as they sink. Why does that help their carbon reach the seafloor?

options.label: Clumps float until currents carry them to shore
Clumps sink faster, escaping being eaten or decomposed
Clumps are too hard for any bacteria to digest
Clumps trap air that pulls them downward

items.explain: Aggregation greatly speeds sinking, giving particles a better chance of escaping predation and decomposition on the way down.

items.prompt: Of all the particles that sink out of the surface ocean, roughly what share reaches the seabed?

options.label: About 1%
About 25%
About half
Nearly all of them

items.explain: Only about 1% of particles leaving the surface reach the seabed; most are consumed or respired on the way.

items.prompt: A coccolithophore builds itself a protective calcium carbonate coating. Which part of the pump does that coating feed?

options.label: The soft-tissue pump
The physical pump
The nitrogen pump
The carbonate pump

items.explain: Calcium carbonate formed into shells and coatings is cycled by the carbonate pump; organic matter goes through the soft-tissue pump.

items.prompt: Upwelling regions fix 2 to 3 times more carbon per area than the open ocean. Why does the open ocean still fix most of the ocean's carbon?

options.label: It covers far more of the ocean's area
Its plankton work faster in deep water
Upwelling regions only work in winter
Its water holds more dissolved oxygen

items.explain: The open ocean makes up more than 90% of the ocean's area, so it fixes about 80% of the carbon despite lower output per area.

items.prompt: Carbon carried into the deep ocean as dissolved inorganic carbon does not stay there forever. How does it get back to the air?

options.label: Storms churn it up within a few weeks
Deep ocean circulation returns it over millennia
Fish carry it up on their nightly swims
Undersea volcanoes blast it to the surface

items.explain: Thermohaline circulation brings deep-ocean dissolved inorganic carbon back to the atmosphere on timescales of thousands of years.

paragraphs.heading: Life that buries carbon
paragraphs.text: The biological pump is the set of living processes by which the ocean moves carbon from the air and from land runoff down into its interior and into seafloor sediments. Put simply, life locks carbon away in the deep sea, out of reach of the atmosphere and the land. It is the biological half of a wider marine carbon pump that also has a physical half. It covers two kinds of cycling: the soft-tissue pump, for organic matter made mostly by phytoplankton through photosynthesis, and the carbonate pump, for the calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) that some plankton and mollusks build into shells.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: The ocean helps regulate how much CO₂ is in the air. Each year the pump carries about 10.2 gigatonnes of carbon into the ocean's interior, keeping it away from the atmosphere for several thousand years or more. Without it, atmospheric carbon dioxide would be about 400 ppm higher than it is now.

paragraphs.heading: Step one, the sunlit surface
paragraphs.text: The pump works in three phases. First, in the sunlit surface layer, called the euphotic zone, phytoplankton use carbon dioxide, nitrogen, phosphorus and trace elements such as iron and zinc to make carbohydrates, fats and proteins. Some plankton, such as coccolithophores and foraminifera, also combine calcium with dissolved carbonates to build a protective coat of calcium carbonate.

paragraphs.heading: Step two, the long fall
paragraphs.text: Once carbon is fixed in soft or hard tissue, the organisms either stay near the surface and get recycled, or die and start sinking. On the way down, particles often clump into aggregates, which fall much faster. Clumping gives them a better chance to avoid being eaten or decomposed before they reach the seafloor. Droppings from larger zooplankton such as copepods can join these fast-sinking clumps.

paragraphs.heading: Step three, recycling and storage
paragraphs.text: Carbon that bacteria decompose, during the fall or on the seafloor, is remineralized so it can be used again for new growth. About 1% of the particles leaving the surface make it to the seabed. Those that escape decomposition are buried in sediment, where carbon can stay for millions of years, and this buried carbon is what ultimately lowers CO₂ in the air. Over thousands of years, thermohaline circulation brings dissolved carbon from the deep ocean back to the atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Small organisms, big totals
paragraphs.text: Marine phytoplankton fix roughly 50–60 Pg of carbon each year, and ocean production accounts for about half of all carbon fixation on Earth. They do this while making up under 1% of the planet's photosynthetic biomass. Rich upwelling regions produce 2 to 3 times more fixed carbon per area, yet about 80% of the fixing happens in the open ocean, because it covers more than 90% of the ocean's area.
